title: Quadratic Equations
description: Comprehensive shared preparation notes and worked practice for Quadratic Equations. Review the target examination syllabus and level before reuse.

sections.label: Concepts and worked examples
sections.html:
Forms and solutions

A quadratic equation is (\(ax^2+bx+c=0\)), where (\(a \neq 0\)). Factoring into two linear factors and using the zero-product property is often fastest. Otherwise, complete the square or apply the quadratic formula.

Formula and discriminant

The roots are (\(x=(-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac})/(2a)\)). The discriminant (\(D=b^2-4ac\)) determines real roots: (\(D>0\)) gives two distinct real roots, (\(D=0\)) one repeated real root, and (\(D<0\)) no real roots.

Root relationships

If roots are (\(r\)) and (\(s\)), then (\(r+s=-b/a\)) and (\(rs=c/a\)). These relationships can answer questions about roots without solving the equation.

Worked example: Solve (\(2x^2-5x+2=0\)). Factor as (\((2x-1)(x-2)=0\)), so (\(x=1/2\)) or (\(x=2\)). Their sum is (\(5/2=-b/a\)) and product is (\(1=c/a\)).

sections.label: Methods and exam checks
sections.html:
• Write all terms on one side and identify (a,b,c), including zero coefficients.
  • Try integer factor pairs when the coefficients are small.
  • Use the discriminant before attempting a full solution if only the number of roots is asked.
  • Do not divide an equation by an expression that could be zero without checking that case.
  • Check roots by substitution into the original equation.

sections.label: Key facts and formulas
sections.html:
• Quadratic formula: (\(x=(-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac})/(2a)\)).
  • Root sum is (\(-b/a\)); root product is (\(c/a\)).
  • A parabola opens upward for (\(a>0\)) and downward for (\(a<0\)).
  • The vertex has x-coordinate (\(-b/(2a)\)).

sections.label: Worked practice
sections.html:
1. Core:

    What are the roots of (\(x^2-5x+6=0\))?

    1. (\(1,6\))
    2. (\(2,3\))
    3. (\(-2,-3\))
    4. (\(3,6\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(2,3\))

    Factor: (\(x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)\)). Thus (\(x=2\)) or (\(x=3\)).

  2. Core:

    How many real roots does (\(x^2+4x+5=0\)) have?

    1. None
    2. One
    3. Two
    4. Infinitely many
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: None

    The discriminant is (\(4^2-4(1)(5)=16-20=-4<0\)), so there are no real roots.

  3. Foundation:

    Solve (\(x^2-9=0\)).

    1. (\(x=3 only\))
    2. (\(x=-3 only\))
    3. (\(x=3 or x=-3\))
    4. (\(x=9 or x=-9\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(x=3 or x=-3\))

    Factor: (\((x-3)(x+3)=0\)). Thus (\(x=3\)) or (\(x=-3\)).

  4. Standard:

    How many distinct real roots does (\(x^2-6x+9=0\)) have?

    1. (\(0\))
    2. (\(1\))
    3. (\(2\))
    4. Infinitely many
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(1\))

    The discriminant is (\((-6)^2-4(1)(9)=36-36=0\)), so there is one repeated real root.

  5. Challenge:

    The roots of (\(x^2-7x+k=0\)) differ by 1. Find (\(k\)).

    1. (\(10\))
    2. (\(12\))
    3. (\(13\))
    4. (\(14\))
    Show answer and solution

    Answer: (\(12\))

    The roots have sum 7 and differ by 1, so they are 3 and 4. Their product is (\(k=12\)).
